Chapter Six: Schools as Mirrors and Windows
Picture yourself walking into a school. You can almost feel the pulse of its culture—not just in the classrooms, but in the hallways, and even in the artwork that hangs on the walls. For some kids, school feels like a mirror. They see themselves reflected in what they learn, in the teachers guiding them, and in the stories they hear every day. But for others? School is more like a window—they’re looking in on someone else’s world, always feeling a bit outside.
There’s a story about a teacher who noticed her students really came alive during a lesson on civil rights. But as she looked around, only a few kids actually recognized themselves in those stories. She realized the textbooks mostly focused on white inventors, artists, and leaders. Meanwhile, her students of color rarely saw their own histories or cultures celebrated. It hit her—the curriculum was quietly sending a message about whose stories truly mattered.
Most schools don’t mean to leave anyone out. But habits and traditions run deep, don’t they? Think about school plays, holiday celebrations, or even the lunch menu. Sometimes, these things can make certain students feel like they don’t quite belong. Maybe a student brings a special dish from home and gets teased for how it smells. Or a child who doesn’t celebrate Christmas feels invisible during all the December festivities. These moments might seem small, but they stack up, shaping who feels at home—and who feels like a guest.
Now, some schools are starting to change that. In one diverse district, a principal simply asked students what they wanted to see in their classrooms. The answers? They were honest and straightforward: more books with characters who looked like them, more lessons about their ancestors, and more teachers who understood their lives. The school took action—they invited community members to share their stories, updated the library, and reimagined holiday events. Not every change was easy. Some parents worried about letting go of old traditions. But something great happened: the sense of belonging started to grow.
For so many kids, the difference between feeling seen and feeling invisible can shape their whole experience at school. When a child hears their language spoken in the hallway, or sees a teacher who shares their background, it sends a powerful message— you belong here. And when those signals are missing? Some students pull back, tune out, or act up.
Schools have this amazing potential to be both mirrors and windows. They can reflect each student’s own life, while also opening up new perspectives. The real challenge? Going beyond token gestures and building a culture where every story is valued. It takes honest reflection, creativity, and a willingness to really listen. But when schools get it right, they become places where every child can truly thrive.
